claim: C. thermocellum bacterial cells measure a few micrometers in length and 500-600 nm in thickness.
source: Low-magnification images of the bacteria indicated a typical view of the elongated cells, measuring a few micrometers in length and 500–600 nm in thickness (Figure 1A), which represents a suitable size for in toto analysis of bacteria by cryo-ET (Ortega et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the measured dimensions of the bacterial cells based on low-magnification cryo-EM images.

claim: C. thermocellum cells have a dense layer surrounding the bacterium visible by cryo-EM.
source: Closer inspection of these bacteria confirmed the presence of a dense layer surrounding the bacterium (Figure 1A, arrowhead).
evidence: Direct observation from cryo-EM imaging showing a dense layer around bacteria.

claim: Cryo-tomograms reveal discrete globular protein densities in the extracellular layer of C. thermocellum.
source: Slices through typical cryo-tomograms (Figure 1B,C) revealed discrete globular protein densities in the extracellular layer and densities that emanate from the bacterial S-layer to this extracellular protein layer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct observation from cryo-tomography data showing protein densities.

claim: The extracellular density layer detected by cryo-EM corresponds to cellulosome complexes.
source: To confirm that the extracellular density layer detected by cryo-ET is composed of cellulosome assemblies, we utilized confocal immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 1D) and immunogold labeling with specific antibody targeting of the cellulose-binding module 3a (CBM3a) component of the CipA (ScaA) scaffoldin (Figure 1E and Video 1), the major defining constituent of the C. thermocellum cellulosome complex.
evidence: Immunofluorescence and immunogold labeling experiments confirm the identity of the extracellular layer.

claim: C. thermocellum mutant strains lacking cellulosomal scaffoldins show complete absence of extracellular densities.
source: Cryo-ET analysis of these mutant bacteria indicated complete absence of extracellular densities (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F) as compared to the wild-type cells.
evidence: Comparison of cryo-ET data between wild-type and mutant strains demonstrates the cellulosomal nature of the extracellular layer.

claim: There is a characteristic gap between the S-layer and the cellulosome layer with an average distance of 64 ± 17 nm.
source: Interestingly, cryo-tomograms of intact C. thermocellum cells revealed a characteristic gap which was not visible in chemically fixed samples between the S-layer and the cellulosome layer, with an average distance of 64 ± 17 nm (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), while the thickness of the cellulosome-rich layer was 65 ± 16 nm (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), measured using bacterial cultures that were cultured for 24 hr.
evidence: Quantitative measurements from cryo-tomograms provide specific distance values.

claim: The thickness of the cellulosome-rich layer is 65 ± 16 nm in bacterial cultures cultured for 24 hr.
source: Interestingly, cryo-tomograms of intact C. thermocellum cells revealed a characteristic gap which was not visible in chemically fixed samples between the S-layer and the cellulosome layer, with an average distance of 64 ± 17 nm (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), while the thickness of the cellulosome-rich layer was 65 ± 16 nm (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), measured using bacterial cultures that were cultured for 24 hr.
evidence: Direct measurement from cryo-tomography data.

claim: Density emanating from the bacterium to the cellulosome layer presumably indicates the anchorage of the cellulosome to the cell wall.
source: Density emanating from the bacterium to the cellulosome layer was detected, which presumably indicated the anchorage of the cellulosome to the cell wall (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, arrows).
evidence: Observation from cryo-tomography with interpretation of the structural feature.

claim: The gap between the S-layer and cellulosome layer is reminiscent of previously described 'contact corridors'.
source: The gap between the S-layer and cellulosome layer is reminiscent of the previously described 'contact corridors' (Bayer and Lamed, 1986), which were proposed to contain anchoring proteins, for example, OlpB (ScaB), that include exceptionally lengthy intermodular linking segments (Bayer and Shimon, 1998; Madkour and Mayer, 2003; Shoham et al., 1999).
evidence: Comparison to previously published work on cellulosome structure.

claim: Cellulosomes form a layer around the bacterium and envelop cellulosic fibers.
source: Strikingly, we observed the cellulosomes, which form a layer around the bacterium and envelop the cellulosic fibers (Figure 2A,B and Video 3).
evidence: Direct observation from VPP-assisted cryo-ET analysis.

claim: Cellulose was identified within the dense cellulosome layer, suggesting a flexible organization of the enzymes.
source: The cellulose was identified within the dense cellulosome layer, suggesting a flexible organization of the enzymes within the cellulosome layer while encompassing the cellulose substrate, presumably offering an advantage for its degradation (Figure 2A,B and Video 3).
evidence: Observation from cryo-ET with interpretation about enzyme organization.

claim: The structure of Cel48S was determined at 3.4 Å resolution by cryo-EM.
source: For this procedure, we purified a recombinant form of the most expressed C. thermocellum dockerin-containing enzyme, which is crucial for enzymatic digestion of MCC, Cel48S (Morag et al., 1991; Raman et al., 2011; Yoav et al., 2017; Zverlov et al., 2005) and determined its structure at 3.4 Å resolution (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Structural determination by cryo-EM with specific resolution reported.

claim: Cel48S is the most expressed C. thermocellum dockerin-containing enzyme.
source: For this procedure, we purified a recombinant form of the most expressed C. thermocellum dockerin-containing enzyme, which is crucial for enzymatic digestion of MCC, Cel48S (Morag et al., 1991; Raman et al., 2011; Yoav et al., 2017; Zverlov et al., 2005) and determined its structure at 3.4 Å resolution (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations about Cel48S expression and function.

claim: Cel48S is crucial for enzymatic digestion of microcrystalline cellulose.
source: For this procedure, we purified a recombinant form of the most expressed C. thermocellum dockerin-containing enzyme, which is crucial for enzymatic digestion of MCC, Cel48S (Morag et al., 1991; Raman et al., 2011; Yoav et al., 2017; Zverlov et al., 2005) and determined its structure at 3.4 Å resolution (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations about Cel48S function.

claim: Enzyme-matching structures were found in close proximity to cellulose and appeared to localize between cellulose chains.
source: The enzyme-matching structures were found in close proximity to the cellulose and appeared to localize between the cellulose chains, presumably, to increase the efficiency of degradation (Figure 2C).
evidence: Template-matching analysis of cryo-tomography data showing enzyme positions.

claim: The architecture of in vitro minicellulosome complex with MCC shows overwhelming resemblance to that found in situ around the bacterium.
source: This in vitro minicellulosome complex was incubated with MCC and analyzed by cryo-ET. The architecture found in this in vitro experiment (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4C, D) shows an overwhelming resemblance to that found in situ around the bacterium, further corroborating our findings (Figure 2C).
evidence: Comparison between in vitro and in situ cryo-ET data.

claim: The structure of cellulose undergoes major organizational changes during interaction with cellulosomes, transforming from well-ordered crystalline structure to deconstructed crystalline packaging.
source: Indeed, our analysis revealed that the structure of cellulose undergoes major organizational changes during the interaction with the cellulosomes, transforming from a well-ordered crystalline cellulose structure (Figure 2E) to deconstructed crystalline packaging (Figure 2F, arrowheads).
evidence: Direct observation from cryo-ET showing structural changes in cellulose.

claim: Two distinct phenotypes of cellulosome organization exist on bacterial cells: high-density and low-density organization.
source: Indeed, while studying the structure of the cellulosomal machinery during cellulose degradation, we observed two distinct phenotypes of cellulosome organization on the bacterial cells, that is, high-density (raw data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Video 2), and low-density organization (raw data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Video 4).
evidence: Direct observation from cryo-EM analysis of bacterial populations.

claim: The distribution of high-density versus low-density phenotypes in stationary-phase culture shows a ratio of 1:5.
source: The distribution of these two phenotypes in the stationary-phase culture shows a ratio of 1:5 (high versus low density).
evidence: Quantification from cryo-EM analysis of bacterial populations.

claim: Upon exposure to fresh medium containing cellulose, a sharp increase in the ratio of the high-density phenotype occurs, followed by a gradual decrease back to a 1:5 ratio.
source: Our analysis revealed that, upon exposure of the bacterial cells to the new environment containing only cellulose, a sharp increase in the ratio of the high-density phenotype occurred, after which a gradual decrease in its concentration was observed back to a 1:5 ratio (Figure 3A).
evidence: Time-course analysis of phenotype ratios during bacterial growth.

claim: 1160 individual cells were analyzed from cultures at five time points after inoculation.
source: We analyzed 1160 individual cells, sampled from cultures at five time points after inoculation, which correspond to different population growth phases (with an average of n = 232 cells per time point).
evidence: Description of the experimental sample size and methodology.

claim: The availability of soluble sugars derived from cellulose degradation is tightly connected to the ratio between the two subpopulations and culture growth stage.
source: Our results revealed that the availability of soluble sugars derived from cellulose degradation is tightly connected to the ratio between the two subpopulations and culture growth stage (Figure 3B).
evidence: Correlation analysis between sugar measurements and phenotype ratios.

claim: At early stages of population growth where soluble sugar availability is low, an increase in the high-density subpopulation occurs.
source: At early stages of population growth, where the availability of soluble sugars is low, an increase in the high-density subpopulation occurs, whereas upon increase in sugar availability with population growth, the ratio of the low-density subpopulation increases (Figure 3B).
evidence: Correlation between sugar availability measurements and phenotype distribution.

claim: Upon increase in sugar availability with population growth, the ratio of the low-density subpopulation increases.
source: At early stages of population growth, where the availability of soluble sugars is low, an increase in the high-density subpopulation occurs, whereas upon increase in sugar availability with population growth, the ratio of the low-density subpopulation increases (Figure 3B).
evidence: Correlation between sugar availability measurements and phenotype distribution.

claim: In late stages of growth when the high-density subpopulation comprises only 20% of the overall population, the soluble sugar concentration remained stable.
source: Interestingly, in the late stages of growth, when the high-density subpopulation comprises only 20% of the overall population, the amount of the soluble sugar concentration remained stable and did not decrease even when the population growth reached its peak.
evidence: Observation from time-course measurements of sugar concentration and phenotype ratios.

claim: A sharp increase in expression of the cellulosomal machinery occurs upon exposure to new environment, which is substantially reduced at early stages of growth and then maintained at basal levels.
source: Our results showed similar dynamics to that of the single-cell phenotypic analysis observed by cryo-EM: that is, a sharp increase in expression of the cellulosomal machinery upon exposure to the new environment, which was substantially reduced at the early stages of growth and then maintained at basal levels.
evidence: RNA and protein expression measurements over time.

claim: The increase in cellulosome expression is corroborated at the RNA levels of Cel48S and CipA.
source: This increase in cellulosome expression was corroborated at the RNA levels of the two major cellulosomal components, Cel48S and CipA (Figure 3C), thus corroborating previous reports (Dror et al., 2003a; Dror et al., 2003b; Ortiz de Ora et al., 2018; Ortiz de Ora et al., 2017), and at the protein level where we quantified the expression levels of CipA, using a specific antibody against its CBM3a component (Figure 3C).
evidence: RNA quantification data supported by previous literature.

claim: Addition of cellobiose at the onset of cellulosomal expression resulted in a negative effect on Cel48S expression.
source: Addition of cellobiose resulted in a negative effect on Cel48S expression, the main cellulosome component (Figure 3D), thereby suggesting that the availability of soluble sugars as products from the cellulose-degradation process is one of the cardinal ways for controlling the expression of cellulosomal components (Figure 4).
evidence: Experimental manipulation showing effect of cellobiose on gene expression.

claim: The availability of soluble sugars as products from cellulose degradation is one of the cardinal ways for controlling the expression of cellulosomal components.
source: Addition of cellobiose resulted in a negative effect on Cel48S expression, the main cellulosome component (Figure 3D), thereby suggesting that the availability of soluble sugars as products from the cellulose-degradation process is one of the cardinal ways for controlling the expression of cellulosomal components (Figure 4).
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing sugar effect on expression.

claim: The basal RNA levels of cellulosomal components at time 54 hr are 20% of the highest expression levels at time 15 hr.
source: In addition, it is interesting to note that the basal expression level of the cellulosome machinery at time 54 hr is 20% of its highest expression levels at time 15 hr (Figure 3C).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of RNA expression levels at different time points.

claim: The basal expression level corresponds to the proportion of the high-density subpopulation in the overall population (20%) at times 0 and 54 hr.
source: This corresponds to the proportion of the high-density subpopulation in the overall population (20%) at times 0 and 54 hr (Figure 3A), thus suggesting that the basal RNA levels stem from the expression of the cellulosome machinery in the high-density cell subpopulations.
evidence: Correlation between expression levels and phenotype proportions.

claim: The distribution of cellulosome density on cell walls exhibited an all-or-none phenotype without observable distribution of intermediate phenotypes.
source: The distribution of cellulosome density on the cell walls exhibited an all-or-none phenotype, where cells were either highly decorated with cellulosomes or almost devoid of cell-surface cellulosomes, without observable distribution of intermediate phenotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B), thus suggesting that cellulosome shedding occurs in an abrupt manner, similar to protein secretion, and not a gradual process during growth.
evidence: Observation from cryo-EM analysis with interpretation about the mechanism.

claim: Cellulosome shedding occurs in an abrupt manner, similar to protein secretion, and not a gradual process during growth.
source: The distribution of cellulosome density on the cell walls exhibited an all-or-none phenotype, where cells were either highly decorated with cellulosomes or almost devoid of cell-surface cellulosomes, without observable distribution of intermediate phenotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B), thus suggesting that cellulosome shedding occurs in an abrupt manner, similar to protein secretion, and not a gradual process during growth.
evidence: Inference from the observed all-or-none phenotype distribution.

claim: A division-of-labor strategy takes place in the C. thermocellum population where the high-density subpopulation expresses costly cellulosome machinery while the low-density subpopulation invests in propagation.
source: Taking our overall findings into account, it is tempting to speculate that a division-of-labor strategy takes place in the C. thermocellum population. In this scenario, the high-density subpopulation expresses the cellulosome machinery comprising enormous amounts of proteins and consequent metabolic costs, thus limiting the resources that this subpopulation can invest in growth, while at the same time the low-density subpopulation does not pay these costs and can invest them in propagation.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed phenotypic heterogeneity.

claim: The findings are consistent with a bet-hedging strategy in the C. thermocellum population mediated by phenotypic heterogeneity.
source: Finally, our findings are consistent with a bet-hedging strategy in the C. thermocellum population, mediated by phenotypic heterogeneity, whereby the presence of diverse phenotypes adapted to different environments would spread the risk of varying environmental conditions (Villa Martín et al., 2019).
evidence: Interpretation of findings in the context of ecological theory with citation.

claim: Plants represent the largest reservoir of biomass on the planet.
source: Plants represent the largest reservoir of biomass on the planet (Bar-On et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Plant cell-wall degradation is essential for carbon recycling, environmental homeostasis, and of major significance to waste management and mammalian gut ecosystems.
source: Hence, plant cell-wall degradation is essential for carbon recycling, environmental homeostasis, and of major significance to waste management and mammalian gut ecosystems.
evidence: Statement based on established scientific knowledge about ecological processes.

claim: Bacteria are central players in plant cell-wall degradation as some are capable of deconstructing cellulosic fibers into simple sugars.
source: Bacteria are central players in this process, as some are capable of deconstructing cellulosic fibers into simple sugars that fuel microbial growth and fermentation cascades essential for nutrient cycling as well as their use in industrial processes (Himmel and Bayer, 2009).
evidence: Statement supported by citation about bacterial cellulose degradation.

claim: Several anaerobic bacteria have evolved energy-effective strategies to solve the challenge of fiber breakdown through the biosynthesis of multienzymatic complexes called cellulosomes.
source: Several anaerobic bacteria have evolved energy-effective strategies to solve the challenge of fiber breakdown through the biosynthesis of multienzymatic complexes called cellulosomes (Artzi et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citation about cellulosome evolution.

claim: Cellulosomes are massive multimodular protein machineries composed of numerous enzymes attached via complementary cohesin-dockerin interactions to scaffoldins.
source: Cellulosomes are massive multimodular protein machineries, composed of numerous enzymes attached via complementary cohesin–dockerin interactions to enzyme-integrating subunits called 'scaffoldins' (Bayer et al., 2004; Fontes and Gilbert, 2010; Lamed et al., 1983b).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations about cellulosome structure.

claim: Genomes of different cellulosome-producing bacterial species can encode up to 200 different types of dockerin-bearing proteins.
source: Genomes of the different cellulosome-producing bacterial species can encode up to 200 different types of dockerin-bearing proteins (notably enzymes) which bind tenaciously to the cohesins of the scaffoldin subunit.
evidence: Statement about genomic content of cellulosome-producing bacteria.

claim: The resultant multiprotein complexes, heterogeneous in their enzyme content, are highly efficient in deconstructing plant cell-wall polysaccharides.
source: The resultant multiprotein complexes, heterogeneous in their enzyme content, are highly efficient in deconstructing plant cell-wall polysaccharides.
evidence: Statement about cellulosome function based on established knowledge.

claim: How cellulosomes are structured and organized on the bacterial cell wall in situ remains largely unknown.
source: Although extensive research has been dedicated to investigate cellulosome activity and its composition in various cellulosome-producing bacteria (Artzi et al., 2017), how cellulosomes are structured and organized on the bacterial cell wall in situ remains largely unknown (Bayer et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement about knowledge gap supported by citations.

claim: Conventional methods have identified structural features of individual cellulosomal modules and crucial interface residues responsible for cohesin-dockerin binding.
source: Conventional methods have identified structural features of individual cellulosomal modules, as well as crucial interface residues that are responsible for the specific tenacious intermodular cohesin–dockerin binding between these definitive cellulosomal modules (Adams et al., 2006; Carvalho et al., 2007; Carvalho et al., 2003; Nash et al., 2016; Noach et al., 2010; Noach et al., 2009; Salama-Alber et al., 2013; Wojciechowski et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of previous structural studies supported by multiple citations.

claim: Larger cellulosome fragments have been structurally studied by crystallography, small-angle X-ray scattering, computational modeling, and negative-staining transmission electron microscopy.
source: In addition, larger cellulosome fragments have been structurally studied by complementary approaches, that is, crystallography, small-angle X-ray scattering, computational modeling, and negative-staining transmission electron microscopy (Bomble et al., 2011; Bule et al., 2018; García-Alvarez et al., 2011; Hammel et al., 2005; Mayer et al., 1987).
evidence: Summary of previous structural studies supported by multiple citations.

claim: Pioneering studies in the 1980s using electron microscopic imaging provided a two-dimensional glimpse into the massive size and organization of the cellulolytic machinery on the bacterial cell surface of C. thermocellum.
source: Pioneering studies published in the 1980s, using electron microscopic imaging, have provided a two-dimensional glimpse into the massive size and organization of the cellulolytic machinery on the bacterial cell surface of C. thermocellum (Artzi et al., 2017; Bayer and Lamed, 1986; Lamed et al., 1983b; Madkour and Mayer, 2003; Mayer et al., 1987).
evidence: Summary of historical studies supported by multiple citations.

claim: Previous electron microscopy studies employed dehydration and chemical fixation procedures which restrict the structural information and characterization of bacterial cell-wall systems.
source: Nevertheless, these studies employed dehydration and chemical fixation procedures, which thus restrict the structural information and characterization of these bacterial cell-wall systems.
evidence: Critique of previous methodologies based on their limitations.

claim: Structural and ecological insights into the in situ fiber-degrading process at the molecular scale while complexes are in their active state remains unknown.
source: Hence, structural and ecological insights into the in situ fiber-degrading process at the molecular scale, while these complexes are in their active state, remains unknown.
evidence: Statement about knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of Cel48S confirmed a previously published X-ray structure of this enzyme.
source: Our data confirmed a previously published X-ray structure of this enzyme (Liu et al., 2018) and added new information regarding the amino acids that link the enzyme to its dockerin and on the interaction of this enzyme with cellulose.
evidence: Comparison of new cryo-EM structure with previously published X-ray structure.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of Cel48S added new information regarding the amino acids that link the enzyme to its dockerin.
source: Our data confirmed a previously published X-ray structure of this enzyme (Liu et al., 2018) and added new information regarding the amino acids that link the enzyme to its dockerin and on the interaction of this enzyme with cellulose.
evidence: New structural information obtained from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: Conformational adaptability of the cellulosome on the cellulose surface was recently observed by atomic force microscopy.
source: Such conformational adaptability of the cellulosome on the cellulose surface was also recently observed by atomic force microscopy (Eibinger et al., 2020).
evidence: Supporting evidence from another study using different methodology.

claim: The detachment of the cellulosomal machinery from the cell surface during culture growth has been reported since its initial discovery.
source: The detachment of the cellulosomal machinery from the cell surface during culture growth has been reported since its initial discovery (Bayer et al., 1985; Lamed et al., 1983a; Lamed et al., 1983b), thus raising questions concerning the extent of this phenomenon and its single-cell distribution across the microbial population, as well as its ecological relevance.
evidence: Historical observation supported by citations.

claim: Phenotypic heterogeneity is considered an important ecological strategy for microorganisms to cope with environmental fluctuations.
source: Phenotypic heterogeneity is considered to be an important ecological strategy for microorganisms to cope with environmental fluctuations and could be mediated by gene expression, where the proportion of cells that express the related phenotype changes as a function of environmental cues (López-Maury et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement about ecological theory supported by citation.

claim: The total cellulolytic activity presents a sharp increase during early growth followed by a sharp decrease in later growth stages.
source: The total cellulolytic activity presents the same pattern, which comprises a sharp increase in activity during early growth, followed by a sharp decrease in later growth stages (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Enzymatic activity measurements over time.

claim: Cellulose degradation is instrumental to the global carbon cycle.
source: Degradation of cellulose, the most abundant organic polymer on Earth, is instrumental to the global carbon cycle.
evidence: Statement about the ecological importance of cellulose degradation based on established knowledge.

claim: Bacterial cells form 'cellulosome capsules' driven by catalytic product-dependent dynamics which can increase the rate of hydrolysis.
source: We reveal that bacterial cells form 'cellulosome capsules' driven by catalytic product-dependent dynamics, which can increase the rate of hydrolysis.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from the study.

claim: Biosynthesis of cellulosomal machinery and cell growth are decoupled at the single-cell level.
source: Biosynthesis of this energetically costly machinery and cell growth are decoupled at the single-cell level, hinting at a division-of-labor strategy through phenotypic heterogeneity.
evidence: Summary statement of findings from the study.

claim: Intrapopulation interactions are key to understanding rates of fiber degradation.
source: This novel observation highlights intrapopulation interactions as key to understanding rates of fiber degradation.
evidence: Interpretive conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: The obtained Cel48S model was compared to the pdb of the Cel48S exoglucanase (5yj6) by fit-in-map option in Chimera, resulting in a correlation score of 0.87.
source: The obtained final model was compared to the pdb of the Cel48S exoglucanase (5yj6, Liu et al., 2018) by the fit-in-map option in Chimera, resulting in a correlation score of 0.87.
evidence: Quantitative comparison of structural models.

claim: The RMSD between amino acids 1 and 663 of the two Cel48S models was 5.7 Å.
source: The RMSD between 1 and 663 amino acids of two models were in 5.7 Å.
evidence: Quantitative structural comparison metric.

claim: At the resolution of individual tomograms, Cel48S cannot be distinguished from other large globular enzymes of the cellulosome.
source: It should be noted that at the resolution of individual tomograms, we cannot distinguish the Cel48S from the other large globular enzymes of the cellulosome.
evidence: Statement about the limitations of the imaging resolution.

claim: The depicted densities in rendered views can be attributed to Cel48S enzyme as well as to additional cellulosome-containing enzymes.
source: Therefore, it is plausible that the depicted densities in our rendered view can be attributed the Cel48S enzyme as well as to additional cellulosome containing enzymes.
evidence: Interpretation acknowledging limitations in enzyme identification.

claim: The contrast of globular cellulolytic enzymes is relatively high in comparison to the flexible rod-like appearance of scaffoldins.
source: Since the contrast of the globular cellulolytic enzymes is relatively high in comparison to the flexible rod-like appearance of scaffoldins, we could not reliably follow the densities of scaffoldins.
evidence: Observation about imaging contrast differences between structural components.

claim: Densities of scaffoldins could not be reliably followed in the tomograms.
source: Since the contrast of the globular cellulolytic enzymes is relatively high in comparison to the flexible rod-like appearance of scaffoldins, we could not reliably follow the densities of scaffoldins.
evidence: Statement about limitations in tracking specific structural components.

claim: The high-density subpopulation serves as a cellulosomal reservoir for future sugar-limiting conditions.
source: Similarly, in our case, although the soluble sugar levels are not limiting at stationary phase (Figure 3B), the high-density cell subpopulation, albeit at lower ratios, still expresses the costly cellulosomal machinery and would therefore provide the first line of defense for a future nutrient-poor and hostile environment containing only cellulose polymers.
evidence: Inference about the ecological function of the high-density phenotype.

claim: The high-density phenotype provides the first line of defense for a future nutrient-poor environment containing only cellulose polymers.
source: Similarly, in our case, although the soluble sugar levels are not limiting at stationary phase (Figure 3B), the high-density cell subpopulation, albeit at lower ratios, still expresses the costly cellulosomal machinery and would therefore provide the first line of defense for a future nutrient-poor and hostile environment containing only cellulose polymers.
evidence: Interpretation of the ecological role of phenotypic heterogeneity.
